blocks.content: Contiguous memory allocation has a fatal flaw. No matter how carefully the operating system packs processes into RAM, free memory eventually breaks into small scattered holes that are individually too small to satisfy new requests, even when the total free space is more than enough. Paging is the idea that fixes this problem completely, and it does so with a single, elegant trick: stop insisting that a process's memory be one contiguous block at all.

This chapter is the central topic of the Memory Management module. It introduces the page table as the data structure paging depends on, walks through address translation step by step with a full worked numeric example, explains why page sizes are almost always a power of two, and covers internal fragmentation, the one cost paging never fully escapes. By the end you should be able to translate a logical address to a physical address by hand, one of the single most common paging interview questions.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408864949-425117590.png
1. Why Paging Exists, the Trouble With Contiguous Allocation
blocks.text: 1. Why Paging Exists, the Trouble With Contiguous Allocation

blocks.content: Before paging, the simplest way an operating system could give a process memory was to hand it one single contiguous block of physical RAM, one unbroken run of addresses large enough to hold the entire process. This is straightforward to implement and easy to reason about, and it works fine as long as processes start and finish in a tidy, predictable order.

The trouble starts once processes are created and destroyed at different times, over and over, for hours or days on end. Every time a process finishes, it leaves behind a hole of free memory exactly the size it used. New processes arrive needing different sized blocks, and after enough churn, free memory ends up scattered across many small holes rather than existing as one large usable stretch. This is external fragmentation: the total free memory is often more than enough for a new request, but no single hole is large enough to satisfy it, because contiguous allocation demands one unbroken chunk.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408864949-509867382.png
blocks.alt: Why Paging Exists, the Trouble With Contiguous Allocation

blocks.content: Paging attacks this problem at its root by removing the contiguous requirement entirely. Instead of demanding one unbroken block, paging allows a process's memory to live in many small, separate, fixed size pieces scattered anywhere across physical RAM. A hole too small to hold an entire process contiguously can still hold one or more of that process's pieces perfectly well, since each piece only needs to be a small fixed size, not the size of the whole process.
2. Pages and Frames, Dividing Both Spaces Into Fixed Size Pieces
blocks.text: 2. Pages and Frames, Dividing Both Spaces Into Fixed Size Pieces

blocks.content: Paging divides a process's logical address space into equal sized pieces called pages. Every page is exactly the same fixed size, commonly 4096 bytes, and a process's entire logical address space is simply page after page laid end to end, numbered 0, 1, 2, and so on upward.

Physical memory is divided the same way, into equal sized pieces called frames. A frame is exactly the same fixed size as a page, so any page from any process can be placed into any free frame anywhere in physical RAM. Crucially, a page and the frame it occupies do not need to be physically adjacent to any other page belonging to the same process. Page 0 of a process might live in frame 3, page 1 in frame 6, and page 2 in frame 2, scattered wherever free frames happen to exist.

This single change eliminates the need for contiguous allocation entirely. Since every page fits into any free frame, memory allocation becomes a matter of finding enough free frames anywhere in RAM, not one giant free stretch. A physical memory riddled with small scattered holes, the exact scenario that defeated contiguous allocation in the previous section, is no longer a problem at all, since those small holes are now perfectly usable frames.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408864950-484189222.png
blocks.alt: Pages and Frames, Dividing Both Spaces Into Fixed Size Pieces

blocks.alt: Pages and Frames, Dividing Both Spaces Into Fixed Size Pieces

blocks.title: In one sentence
blocks.content: Paging splits a process's logical address space into fixed size pages and physical memory into equal sized frames, then maps each page to some frame individually, so a process's pages never need to sit next to each other in physical memory.
3. The Page Table, Mapping Pages to Frames
blocks.text: 3. The Page Table, Mapping Pages to Frames

blocks.content: Once a process's pages are scattered across frames with no guaranteed pattern, the operating system needs some way to remember exactly which frame each page actually landed in. That record is called the page table, and it is the single data structure that makes paging work at all.

A page table holds exactly one entry per page. Each entry stores the frame number that page currently occupies in physical memory. To find out where page 2 of a process lives, the hardware simply looks at entry number 2 in that process's page table and reads off the frame number stored there, nothing more complicated than an array lookup.

Every process has its own separate page table. Two different processes can both have a page 0, a page 1, and so on, and their page tables will almost certainly point those identically numbered pages at completely different frames. This is exactly what allows two processes, both compiled as if they start at logical address zero, to coexist safely in the same physical RAM without ever colliding.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865181-967923372.png
blocks.alt: The Page Table, Mapping Pages to Frames

blocks.title: One page table per process
blocks.content: A page table is never shared between processes. When the operating system switches from running one process to another, it also switches which page table the hardware uses for translation, exactly the same way it switches every other piece of that process's state.
4. Address Translation Step by Step

Translating a logical address into a physical address under paging follows a fixed, mechanical procedure, performed by hardware on every single memory access. The first step is splitting the logical address itself into two separate parts: a page number and an offset within that page.

The page number identifies which page of the process this address falls inside, and the offset identifies exactly how far into that page the address sits, counted from the page's own starting byte. Both numbers come from the exact same logical address, just split apart, with the page number occupying the higher order bits and the offset occupying the lower order bits.

Once the page number is known, it is used to index directly into that process's page table, reading off the frame number stored there. The final physical address is then computed by combining that frame number with the same offset value from the split: the frame tells hardware which fixed size block of physical RAM to use, and the offset tells it exactly how far into that block to go.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865181-739286480.png
The offset never changes during translation. Only the page number is replaced by a frame number, everything else about the address stays exactly where it was inside its page.
5. A Worked Example, Translating Logical Address 5000
blocks.text: 5. A Worked Example, Translating Logical Address 5000

blocks.content: Numbers make this concrete faster than any explanation. Assume a page size of 4096 bytes, 4 KB, a completely standard size on real hardware, and assume a process generates the logical address 5000 during execution.

Dividing 5000 by 4096 gives a page number of 1, since 4096 fits into 5000 exactly once with something left over. That leftover, 904, is the offset: it is exactly how far past the start of page 1 this particular byte sits.

{"headers":["Quantity","Value"],"rows":[["Logical address","5000"],["Page size","4096 bytes"],["Page number","1"],["Offset","904"],["Frame number, from the page table","6"],["Physical address","25480"]]}

Looking up page 1 in the example page table from the previous section gives frame number 6. Combining that frame number with the offset produces the real physical address: 6 multiplied by the page size, 4096, gives 24576, and adding the offset, 904, gives a final physical address of 25480. That is the real RAM location the hardware actually touches, even though the running program only ever knew about address 5000.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865181-37008675.png
blocks.alt: A Worked Example, Translating Logical Address 5000

blocks.content: 6. Why Page Size Is Almost Always a Power of Two
blocks.text: 6. Why Page Size Is Almost Always a Power of Two

blocks.content: Every worked example so far used a page size of 4096 bytes, and that is not a coincidence. Page sizes on real hardware are almost always a power of two, values like 4096, 8192, or 16384, and the reason is entirely about how cheap the splitting step becomes in hardware.

When the page size is a power of two, splitting a logical address into a page number and an offset stops being a division and a remainder calculation at all. It becomes a bit shift and a bit mask, two of the fastest operations any processor can perform, executed in a single clock cycle rather than the many cycles a true division would cost.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865182-632307778.png
blocks.alt: Why Page Size Is Almost Always a Power of Two

blocks.content:
// with a page size that is a power of two, division and remainder
// become simple bit operations instead of real arithmetic

page_size = 4096;              // 4096 equals 2 raised to the power 12
shift_amount = 12;             // log base 2 of 4096
offset_mask = 4095;            // the low 12 bits, all set to 1

page_number = logical_address >> shift_amount;   // shift right by 12 bits
offset      = logical_address & offset_mask;     // keep only the low 12 bits

blocks.content: A bit shift costs one clock cycle. A true division can cost dozens. Since translation happens on every single memory access, that difference is the reason page sizes are powers of two.
7. Internal Fragmentation, Paging's Own Unavoidable Cost
blocks.text: 7. Internal Fragmentation, Paging's Own Unavoidable Cost

blocks.content: Paging solves external fragmentation completely, but it introduces a smaller cost of its own called internal fragmentation. A process's total size is almost never an exact multiple of the page size, which means its very last page is usually only partially filled with real data.

The unused remainder inside that last page cannot be handed to any other process. It is reserved as part of this process's final page whether it holds useful data or not, and it simply sits wasted until the process finishes and that page is freed. Unlike external fragmentation, this waste is trapped inside memory that has already been allocated, not scattered as separate unusable holes.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865182-896018422.png
blocks.alt: Internal Fragmentation, Paging's Own Unavoidable Cost

blocks.title: How much gets wasted on average
blocks.content: Across many processes with random sizes, the amount wasted inside each one's last page averages out to roughly half a page. A single process might waste far less or, in the worst case, nearly an entire page, but half a page per process is the standard textbook estimate.
8. Paging versus Contiguous Allocation at a Glance
blocks.text: 8. Paging versus Contiguous Allocation at a Glance

blocks.content: With both approaches now fully explained, the contrast between them is worth lining up directly.

{"headers":["Aspect","Contiguous Allocation","Paging"],"rows":[["Fragmentation type","External fragmentation, scattered unusable holes","Internal fragmentation, wasted space inside the last page"],["Allocation flexibility","Requires one unbroken block of matching size","Any free frame anywhere in RAM will do"],["Address translation cost","One addition, base register plus logical address","Extra page table lookup, made fast by the TLB"],["Memory reuse after a process exits","Leaves a hole that may not fit future requests","Leaves individual free frames that always fit"]]}

Paging trades a fragmentation problem it cannot fully solve, tiny internal fragmentation, for one it eliminates completely, external fragmentation, while adding one extra layer of lookup work per memory access that hardware then has to make fast.
9. Hardware Support and the TLB

The page table lookup described in section four is not free. In the most literal implementation, the page table itself lives in physical RAM, which means every single memory access a program makes would actually require two real memory accesses: one to read the page table entry, and a second to read the actual data at the translated physical address. That would roughly double the cost of every memory access in the entire system.

Real hardware avoids this cost with a small, extremely fast cache built directly into the CPU called the Translation Lookaside Buffer, almost always shortened to TLB. The TLB stores the most recently used page number to frame number mappings, so that most translations never need to touch the page table in RAM at all, the answer is usually already sitting in this on chip cache.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785408865182-602988943.png

The full mechanics of how the TLB works, what happens on a hit versus a miss, and how it is kept consistent when a page table changes, are covered in complete depth in the dedicated TLB chapter. This chapter only needs you to understand why the TLB has to exist at all: without it, paging's extra lookup step would be too slow to use in practice.
10. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle
A handful of mistakes come up constantly once this topic reaches practice, and they are worth naming directly.

["Confusing a page with a frame. A page is a fixed size piece of a process's own logical address space. A frame is the corresponding fixed size piece of physical memory. A page is not physically the same thing as the frame it happens to occupy, it is simply mapped there by the page table.","Using the wrong page size in the splitting calculation. If the actual page size is 4096 bytes, dividing by any other number produces a page number and offset that do not correspond to anything real in the page table.","Forgetting that the page size must be a power of two for the bit shifting trick from section six to work at all. If a page size is not a power of two, hardware has no choice but to fall back to genuine division, which is far slower.","Assuming paging removes fragmentation entirely. It removes external fragmentation completely, but internal fragmentation, wasted space inside a process's own last page, is a cost paging can reduce with smaller pages but never fully escape."]
items: Confusing a page with a frame. A page is a fixed size piece of a process's own logical address space. A frame is the corresponding fixed size piece of physical memory. A page is not physically the same thing as the frame it happens to occupy, it is simply mapped there by the page table.

Using the wrong page size in the splitting calculation. If the actual page size is 4096 bytes, dividing by any other number produces a page number and offset that do not correspond to anything real in the page table.

Forgetting that the page size must be a power of two for the bit shifting trick from section six to work at all. If a page size is not a power of two, hardware has no choice but to fall back to genuine division, which is far slower.

Assuming paging removes fragmentation entirely. It removes external fragmentation completely, but internal fragmentation, wasted space inside a process's own last page, is a cost paging can reduce with smaller pages but never fully escape.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to perform a full logical address to physical address translation by hand: given a page size, a logical address, and a small page table, compute the page number, the offset, look up the frame number, and combine it into a physical address, exactly as done in section five. This exact calculation is one of the most commonly asked operating systems interview and exam questions, and interviewers expect the arithmetic to be fast and correct.

Paging is the foundation the rest of this module builds on. Page tables, the TLB, and virtual memory are all extensions of the same core idea introduced here: divide memory into fixed size pieces, and map them individually instead of demanding one contiguous block.
